title: Secure Communication Protocols
subtitle: SSH, JWT signing, TOTP, and secure API authentication

whyItExists.problem: Connecting to servers, issuing API tokens, and implementing 2FA each require applying cryptographic primitives in a specific, correct sequence. Getting any step wrong (e.g., using the wrong JWT algorithm, weak SSH keys, or non-TOTP 2FA) creates exploitable vulnerabilities.
whyItExists.solution: Established protocols (SSH, JWT, TOTP/HOTP) encode the correct sequence of cryptographic operations, parameter choices, and security checks. Using proven implementations is safer than assembling primitives yourself.
whyItExists.whenToUse: SSH for server access, JWTs for stateless API authentication, TOTP for 2FA, HMAC-signed tokens for API keys.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Do not use JWTs to store sensitive data (they are base64, not encrypted, unless you use JWE). Do not implement your own authentication protocol from scratch.

explainModes.beginner: These are pre-built, proven ways to prove identity or protect communication. SSH lets you log into servers safely. JWTs let APIs recognize you without looking up a database on every request. TOTP generates those 6-digit codes that change every 30 seconds.
explainModes.simple: SSH uses public-key cryptography for authentication — your private key proves you are you, without sending a password. JWTs are signed JSON tokens a server issues to prove who you are. TOTP generates time-based codes from a shared secret.
explainModes.standard: SSH: Ed25519 or RSA key pairs; server verifies client's public key against authorized_keys. JWT: header.payload.signature — HS256 (HMAC) for single-service, RS256/ES256 (asymmetric) for multi-service. TOTP: HMAC-SHA1 of shared_secret + time_counter, 6-digit output per RFC 6238.
explainModes.technical: SSH handshake: Diffie-Hellman key exchange → symmetric session key → public key authentication (client proves possession of private key by signing a challenge). JWT vulnerabilities: alg:none attack, RS256→HS256 confusion attack, weak HS256 secrets. TOTP window: ±1 step (±30s) for clock drift tolerance.
explainModes.deepDive: JWT alg:none attack: some libraries that accept multiple algorithms will verify a token with 'alg':'none' as always valid — always whitelist algorithms explicitly. RS256→HS256 confusion: if a library that expects RS256 receives a JWT with alg:HS256 and verifies it using the public key as the HMAC secret, an attacker with the public key can forge tokens. TOTP: HOTP (counter-based) is the base; TOTP adds time = floor(unix_time / 30) as the counter.

content.text: SSH uses public-key cryptography for authentication. Your private key proves your identity without ever sending a password over the network. The server stores your public key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and verifies that you can produce a signature matching it.

content.code:
# --- Generate Ed25519 key pair (recommended) ---
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your@email.com" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
# -C: comment for identification  -f: output file

# --- Generate RSA key pair (if Ed25519 not supported) ---
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your@email.com"

# --- Copy public key to server ---
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub user@server.com
# or manually: cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (on server)

# --- Verify key fingerprint (confirm server identity on first connect) ---
ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub

# --- Secure SSH server config (/etc/ssh/sshd_config) ---
# PasswordAuthentication no       <- disable password login
# PermitRootLogin no              <- never allow root SSH
# AllowUsers youruser             <- whitelist users
# PubkeyAuthentication yes
# AuthorizedKeysFile .ssh/authorized_keys
# Protocol 2                      <- SSHv1 is broken
# KexAlgorithms curve25519-sha256@libssh.org  <- prefer modern key exchange

sudo systemctl restart sshd  # apply changes

content.text: JWTs are signed JSON tokens for stateless API authentication. Format: base64url(header).base64url(payload).signature. The server signs the token; any service that knows the key (HS256) or has the public key (RS256/ES256) can verify it without a database lookup.

content.code:
import jwt
import datetime
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import Ed25519PrivateKey

# --- HS256: symmetric (single service) ---
SECRET = "super-secret-key-at-least-256-bits-long"

payload = {
    "sub": "user:1234",
    "role": "admin",
    "iat": datetime.datetime.utcnow(),
    "exp": datetime.datetime.utcnow() + datetime.timedelta(hours=1),
    "jti": __import__('secrets').token_hex(16)  # unique ID prevents replay
}

token = jwt.encode(payload, SECRET, algorithm="HS256")
print("Token:", token)

# Verify (always specify allowed algorithms — prevents alg:none attack)
decoded = jwt.decode(token, SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])
print("User:", decoded["sub"])

# --- RS256: asymmetric (multiple services) ---
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization

private_key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
public_key_pem = private_key.public_key().public_bytes(
    serialization.Encoding.PEM, serialization.PublicFormat.SubjectPublicKeyInfo
)

# Auth service signs with private key
token_rs256 = jwt.encode(payload, private_key, algorithm="RS256")

# Any service verifies with public key (never needs the private key)
decoded_rs256 = jwt.decode(token_rs256, public_key_pem, algorithms=["RS256"])
print("Verified by any service:", decoded_rs256["sub"])

content.text: Always whitelist algorithms when decoding JWTs: algorithms=["RS256"]. Never use algorithms=["RS256", "HS256"] together — this enables the RS256→HS256 confusion attack where an attacker uses your public key as an HS256 secret to forge tokens.

TOTP (RFC 6238) generates 6-digit codes that change every 30 seconds from a shared secret. It is the basis of Google Authenticator, Authy, and hardware tokens. The server and client independently compute HMAC-SHA1(secret + current_time_step) and compare results.

content.code:
import pyotp  # pip install pyotp
import qrcode  # pip install qrcode[pil]

# --- Setup: generate secret for a new user ---
secret = pyotp.random_base32()  # 32-char base32 secret
print("Store in DB (encrypted):", secret)

# --- Generate QR code for authenticator app ---
totp = pyotp.TOTP(secret)
uri = totp.provisioning_uri(name="user@example.com", issuer_name="MyApp")
qr = qrcode.make(uri)
qr.save("qr.png")

# --- Verify a 6-digit code ---
def verify_totp(user_secret: str, code: str) -> bool:
    t = pyotp.TOTP(user_secret)
    # valid_window=1 allows ±30 seconds for clock drift
    return t.verify(code, valid_window=1)

# Example: user submits "123456"
if verify_totp(secret, "123456"):
    print("2FA valid")
else:
    print("2FA invalid or expired")

# --- HOTP (counter-based OTP, e.g. hardware tokens) ---
hotp = pyotp.HOTP(secret)
print("Code for counter 0:", hotp.at(0))
print("Code for counter 1:", hotp.at(1))

a.name: HS256 (HMAC-SHA256)
a.description: Symmetric — same secret for signing and verifying
weaknesses: All services that verify tokens must know the secret
Secret exposure means all tokens can be forged
a.useWhen: Single service issues AND verifies tokens (monolith, single API)

b.name: RS256 / ES256 (Asymmetric)
b.description: Asymmetric — private key signs, public key verifies
strengths: Verification services never see the signing key
Public key can be published (JWKS endpoint)
One key pair for many verifying services
b.useWhen: OAuth 2.0 / OIDC, microservices, any multi-service verification

content.text: JWTs are not encrypted by default — the payload is just base64-encoded and readable by anyone. Never put sensitive data (SSNs, credit card numbers, passwords) in a JWT payload. Use JWE if you need an encrypted token.

questions.question: Why should you disable PasswordAuthentication in SSH?
options: Password authentication is slower than key authentication
Passwords can be brute-forced; key-based auth requires the private key which never crosses the network
Password auth requires root access on the server
SSH passwords cannot be longer than 32 characters
questions.explanation: SSH passwords can be brute-forced over the network. With key authentication, the private key never leaves the client — the server only receives a cryptographic signature.

questions.question: What is the alg:none JWT attack?
options: An attack that removes the signature from a JWT
Setting the algorithm to 'none' makes some libraries skip signature verification entirely
An attack that replaces HS256 with a weaker algorithm
An attack that guesses the HMAC secret
questions.explanation: Some JWT libraries that accept multiple algorithms will treat alg:none as valid, skipping signature verification. Always whitelist exactly the algorithms you expect.

questions.question: What is TOTP based on?
options: Asymmetric encryption with a user's public key
HMAC of a shared secret and the current 30-second time window
A random number generated by the server on each login
SMS delivery of a one-time password
questions.explanation: TOTP computes HMAC-SHA1(shared_secret, floor(unix_time / 30)). Both the server and authenticator app know the secret and time, so they compute the same 6-digit code independently.

faq.q: What algorithm should I use to sign JWTs in production?
faq.a: RS256 (RSA-SHA256) or ES256 (ECDSA-P256) for services where multiple parties verify tokens. HS256 for a single service that both signs and verifies. Never use RS256 and HS256 in the same library configuration — it enables key confusion attacks.

faq.q: Are JWTs safe to store in localStorage?
faq.a: They are vulnerable to XSS attacks — any JavaScript on the page can read localStorage. Use HttpOnly cookies instead: they cannot be accessed by JavaScript. If you must use localStorage, ensure you have strong XSS prevention.

Yes, in a real-time phishing attack. A phishing page can collect both the password and TOTP code from the user and immediately use them on the real site within the 30-second window. FIDO2/WebAuthn (passkeys) is phishing-resistant. TOTP is still much better than no 2FA.

examples: GitHub requires Ed25519 or ECDSA SSH keys; RSA-1024 and DSA keys were deprecated in 2021
Auth0 and Okta issue RS256 JWTs and publish their public key at a JWKS endpoint for verification
Google Authenticator, Authy, and Microsoft Authenticator all implement TOTP (RFC 6238)
